Default to Farfield\n\n        # --- Device-side data (for computation) ---\n        \n        # Update Mesh Metric Arrays on Device\n        self.mesh.rx = wp.array(self.mesh.rx_host, dtype=wp.float32, device=self.device)\n        self.mesh.ry = wp.array(self.mesh.ry_host, dtype=wp.float32, device=self.device)\n        self.mesh.sx = wp.array(self.mesh.sx_host, dtype=wp.float32, device=self.device)\n        self.mesh.sy = wp.array(self.mesh.sy_host, dtype=wp.float32, device=self.device)\n        self.mesh.J  = wp.array(self.mesh.J_host, dtype=wp.float32, device=self.device)\n        \n        self.face_geo_factors = wp.array(self.face_geo_factors_host, dtype=wp.float32, device=self.device)\n        self.bc_mask = wp.array(self.bc_mask_host, dtype=wp.int32, device=self.device)\n        \n        self.x = wp.array(self.x_host, dtype=wp.float32, device=self.device)\n        self.y = wp.array(self.y_host, dtype=wp.float32, device=self.device)\n\n        # Inverse of Mass Matrix (diagonal)\n        weights_2d = np.kron(self.basis.weights_1d.numpy(), self.basis.weights_1d.numpy())\n        M_inv_diag_host = 1.0 / weights_2d\n        self.M_inv_diag = wp.array(M_inv_diag_host, dtype=wp.float32, device=self.device)\n\n        # Solution field\n        Q_host = np.zeros((mesh.num_elements, basis.Np, 4), dtype=np.float32)\n        self._set_initial_conditions(Q_host, initial_conditions_func)\n        self.Q = wp.array(Q_host, dtype=wp.vec4, device=self.device)\n        self.Q_stage1 = wp.zeros_like(self.Q)\n        self.Q_stage2 = wp.zeros_like(self.Q)\n        self.Q_rk = self.Q # Input for the RHS computation\n        self.rhs = wp.zeros_like(self.Q)\n\n        self.max_wave_speed = wp.zeros(1, dtype=wp.float32, device=self.device)\n\n\n    def _calculate_geometric_factors(self):\n        \"\"\"\n        Calculates geometric factors for affine quadrilateral elements.\n        The transformation is x(r,s) = sum(N_i(r,s) * x_i), where N_i are bilinear shape functions.\n        For affine elements, the derivatives (and thus the Jacobian) are constant.\n        \"\"\"\n        # Derivatives of bilinear shape functions at the center (r=0, s=0)\n        dNd_r_center = 0.25 * np.array([-1, 1, 1, -1])\n        dNd_s_center = 0.25 * np.array([-1, -1, 1, 1])\n        \n        for i in range(self.mesh.num_elements):\n            # vertices are on host, so we use the host array\n            v = self.mesh.vertices_host[i, :, :] \n            dx_dr = dNd_r_center @ v[:, 0]\n            dx_ds = dNd_s_center @ v[:, 0]\n            dy_dr = dNd_r_center @ v[:, 1]\n            dy_ds = dNd_s_center @ v[:, 1]\n            \n            # Jacobian Determinant\n            J = dx_dr * dy_ds - dx_ds * dy_dr\n            \n            # Store J\n            self.mesh.J_host[i] = J\n            \n            # Inverse Jacobian components (dr/dx, dr/dy, etc.)\n            # [dr/dx  dr/dy] = (1/J) * [ dy/ds  -dx/ds]\n            # [ds/dx  ds/dy]           [-dy/dr   dx/dr]\n            dr_dx =  dy_ds / J\n            dr_dy = -dx_ds / J\n            ds_dx = -dy_dr / J\n            ds_dy =  dx_dr / J\n            \n            self.mesh.rx_host[i] = dr_dx\n            self.mesh.ry_host[i] = dr_dy\n            self.mesh.sx_host[i] = ds_dx\n            self.mesh.sy_host[i] = ds_dy\n\n            self.geo_factors_host[i, 0] = dx_dr\n            self.geo_factors_host[i, 1] = dx_ds\n            self.geo_factors_host[i, 2] = dy_dr\n            self.geo_factors_host[i, 3] = dy_ds\n            self.geo_factors_host[i, 4] = J\n            \n            # --- Face geometric factors ---\n            # Face 0 (bottom): s=-1, tangent t = (dx/dr, dy/dr) -> Normal n = (dy/dr, -dx/dr)\n            nx, ny = dy_dr, -dx_dr\n            J_face = np.sqrt(nx**2 + ny**2)\n            self.face_geo_factors_host[i, 0, :] = [nx/J_face, ny/J_face, J_face]\n\n            # Face 1 (right): r=1, tangent t = (dx/ds, dy/ds) -> Normal n = (dy/ds, -dx/ds)\n            nx, ny = dy_ds, -dx_ds\n            J_face = np.sqrt(nx**2 + ny**2)\n            self.face_geo_factors_host[i, 1, :] = [nx/J_face, ny/J_face, J_face]\n            \n            # Face 2 (top): s=1, tangent t = -(dx/dr, dy/dr) -> Normal n = -(dy/dr, -dx/dr) = (-dy/dr, dx/dr)\n            nx, ny = -dy_dr, dx_dr \n            self.face_geo_factors_host[i, 2, :] = [nx/J_face, ny/J_face, J_face]\n\n            # Face 3 (left): r=-1, vector from 3 to 0 (top to bottom).\n            # Tangent is -(dx/ds, dy/ds).\n            # Normal is (-dy/ds, dx/ds).\n            nx, ny = -dy_ds, dx_ds \n            self.face_geo_factors_host[i, 3, :] = [nx/J_face, ny/J_face, J_face]\n\n\n    def _map_nodes_to_physical_space(self):\n        \"\"\" Maps nodal points from the reference to the physical element. \"\"\"\n        r = self.basis.nodes_2d.numpy()[:, 0]; s = self.basis.nodes_2d.numpy()[:, 1]\n        N1 = 0.25*(1-r)*(1-s); N2 = 0.25*(1+r)*(1-s); N3 = 0.25*(1+r)*(1+s); N4 = 0.25*(1-r)*(1+s)\n        N = np.vstack([N1, N2, N3, N4])\n        for i in range(self.mesh.num_elements):\n            v = self.mesh.vertices_host[i, :, :]\n            self.x_host[i, :] = N.T @ v[:, 0]\n            self.y_host[i, :] = N.T @ v[:, 1]\n\n    def _set_initial_conditions(self, Q_host, func):\n        for i in range(self.mesh.num_elements):\n            for j in range(self.basis.Np):\n                rho, u, v, p = func(self.x_host[i, j], self.y_host[i, j])\n                Q_host[i, j, :] = eq.primitive_to_conservative([rho, u, v, p])\n\n    def _compute_rhs(self):\n        \"\"\" Computes the right-hand side of the ODE using Warp kernels. \"\"\"\n        self.rhs.zero_()\n        \n        # --- Volume Integral ---\n        wp.launch(\n            kernel=wk.compute_volume_term,\n            dim=(self.mesh.num_elements, self.basis.Np),\n            inputs=[\n                self.Q_rk,\n                self.rhs,\n                self.basis.Dr,\n                self.basis.Ds,\n                self.mesh.rx,\n                self.mesh.ry,\n                self.mesh.sx,\n                self.mesh.sy,\n                self.basis.Np\n            ],\n            device=self.device\n        )\n        \n        # --- Surface Integral ---\n        wp.launch(\n            kernel=wk.compute_surface_term,\n            dim=self.mesh.num_elements,  # Nur 1 Thread pro Element (Kernel loopt über Faces)\n            inputs=[\n                self.Q_rk,\n                self.rhs,\n                self.mesh.connectivity,\n                self.basis.face_nodes,\n                self.basis.LIFT,\n                self.face_geo_factors, \n                self.mesh.J,\n                self.bc_mask, # Pass BC Types\n                self.basis.Nfp\n            ],\n            device=self.device\n        )\n\n    def solve(self, t_final, CFL, log_frequency=10, writer=None):\n        \"\"\" The main time-stepping loop. \"\"\"\n        t = 0.0\n        step = 0\n        \n        # --- Debugging: Directory to save step-by-step results ---\n        # Only used if no writer is provided\n        output_steps_dir = \"data/steps\"\n        if writer is None and not os.path.exists(output_steps_dir):\n            os.makedirs(output_steps_dir)\n        \n        use_stream = self.device == \"cuda\"\n        if use_stream:\n            stream = wp.Stream(device=self.device)\n\n        while t < t_final:\n            \n            # --- Adaptive dt calculation ---\n            self.max_wave_speed.zero_()\n            wp.launch(\n                kernel=wk.compute_max_wave_speed,\n                dim=(self.mesh.num_elements, self.basis.Np),\n                inputs=[self.Q, self.max_wave_speed],\n                device=self.device\n            )\n            max_speed = self.max_wave_speed.numpy()[0]\n            # print(f\"Max speed: {max_speed:.4e}\")\n            \n            # Ensure max_speed is not zero to avoid division by zero\n            # Also, handle the case where the simulation might start with zero velocity\n            if max_speed < 1.0e-6:\n                max_speed = 1.0 \n\n            # Smallest distance between any two nodes in the mesh (characteristic length)\n            # A simpler but less robust way is to use dx = mesh.lx / mesh.nx\n            dx = self.mesh.dx \n            dt = CFL * dx / max_speed\n            # print(f\"Calculated dt: {dt:.4e}\")\n\n            # --- End of adaptive dt calculation ---\n\n            if use_stream:\n                with stream:\n                    # Standard SSP-RK3 scheme\n                    self.Q_rk = self.Q\n                    self._compute_rhs()\n                    wp.launch(kernel=wk.rk_stage_1, dim=self.Q.shape, inputs=[self.Q, self.rhs, dt], outputs=[self.Q_stage1], device=self.device)\n                    \n                    self.Q_rk = self.Q_stage1\n                    self._compute_rhs()\n                    wp.launch(kernel=wk.rk_stage_2, dim=self.Q.shape, inputs=[self.Q, self.Q_stage1, self.rhs, dt], outputs=[self.Q_stage2], device=self.device)\n\n                    self.Q_rk = self.Q_stage2\n                    self._compute_rhs()\n                    wp.launch(kernel=wk.rk_stage_3, dim=self.Q.shape, inputs=[self.Q, self.Q_stage2, self.rhs, dt], outputs=[self.Q], device=self.device)\n                \n                stream.synchronize()\n            else: # Synchronous execution for CPU\n                # 1st stage\n                self.Q_rk = self.Q\n                self._compute_rhs()\n                wp.launch(kernel=wk.rk_stage_1, dim=self.Q.shape, inputs=[self.Q, self.rhs, dt], outputs=[self.Q_stage1], device=self.device)\n                \n                # 2nd stage\n                self.Q_rk = self.Q_stage1\n                self._compute_rhs()\n                wp.launch(kernel=wk.rk_stage_2, dim=self.Q.shape, inputs=[self.Q, self.Q_stage1, self.rhs, dt], outputs=[self.Q_stage2], device=self.device)\n\n                # 3rd stage\n                self.Q_rk = self.Q_stage2\n                self._compute_rhs()\n                wp.launch(kernel=wk.rk_stage_3, dim=self.Q.shape, inputs=[self.Q, self.Q_stage2, self.rhs, dt], outputs=[self.Q], device=self.device)\n\n                # For CPU, a manual synchronize is good practice to ensure completion\n                wp.synchronize()\n\n\n            t += dt\n            step += 1\n\n            # --- Debugging: Check for NaNs and save step data ---\n            if step % log_frequency == 0:\n                q_np = self.Q.numpy()\n                if np.isnan(q_np).any():\n                    print(f\"!!! Simulation became unstable with NaN values at step {step} (t={t:.4f}).\")\n                    break\n                \n                if writer:\n                    writer.write_step(step, t, q_np)\n                else:\n                    step_filename = os.path.join(output_steps_dir, f\"step_{step:04d}.npz\")\n                    np.savez(step_filename, q=q_np, x=self.x.numpy(), y=self.y.numpy(), vertices=self.mesh.vertices_host)\n\n                print(f\"Step: {step}, t = {t:.4f} / {t_final}, dt = {dt:.3e}\")\n"
  }
}

Q_n\n    q_2: wp.array(dtype=wp.vec4, ndim=2),    # Q(2) aus Stage 2\n    rhs: wp.array(dtype=wp.vec4, ndim=2),    # RHS(Q(2))\n    dt: wp.float32,\n    q_out: wp.array(dtype=wp.vec4, ndim=2)   # Ziel für Q(n+1) (überschreibt oft self.Q)\n    ):\n    \"\"\"\n    Stage 3: Q(n+1) = 1/3 * Q_n + 2/3 * (Q(2) + dt * RHS(Q(2)))\n    \"\"\"\n    e, i = wp.tid()\n    # ✨ ## MODEL

To add a Navier-Stokes (NS) solver to the existing Discontinuous Galerkin architecture, the following files and components would need modification. The primary challenge in DG for Navier-Stokes is handling the second-order diffusion terms (viscosity), which usually requires an approach like the **Interior Penalty (IP)** method or the **Local Discontinuous Galerkin (LDG)** method.

### 1. `src/kernels/warp_kernels.py` (Heavy Modifications)
This file requires the most significant changes to implement the physics on the GPU.
*   **Gradient Kernels (New):** You need to compute the gradients of the primitive variables ($\nabla u, \nabla v, \nabla T$) first. This requires new volume and surface integration kernels specifically for the auxiliary gradient equations (if using LDG/BR2).
*   **Viscous Flux Functions (New):** Implement `@wp.func` for the viscous flux vectors $F_v(Q, \nabla Q)$ and $G_v(Q, \nabla Q)$ containing the stress tensor and heat flux.
*   **Viscous Numerical Flux (New):** Implement the numerical flux function for diffusion (e.g., Interior Penalty flux), which involves jumps in solution, averages of gradients, and a penalty parameter.
*   **Update Main Kernels:** Modify `compute_volume_term` and `compute_surface_term` to include the viscous contributions (subtracting viscous flux from inviscid flux).
*   **Boundary Conditions:** Add logic for **No-Slip Walls** (zero velocity) and thermal BCs (Adiabatic/Isothermal) in the surface kernel.

### 2. `src/core/solver.py` (Structural Logic)
*   **Gradient Variables:** Initialize new Warp arrays to store the gradients ($\sigma$) if using LDG, or intermediate terms.
*   **Two-Step RHS:** The explicit loop needs to change. Instead of just computing RHS from $Q$, you must:
    1.  Compute Gradients $\nabla Q$ from $Q$ (solve auxiliary system).
    2.  Compute RHS from $Q$ and $\nabla Q$.
*   **Time Stepping (CFL):** Update the `dt` calculation. The explicit time step restriction for diffusion scales with $\Delta x^2$ (parabolic), which is much more restrictive than the hyperbolic $\Delta x$ limit. You might need to add a viscosity-based timestep limiter.

### 3. `src/physics/equations.py` (Physics Definitions)
*   **Viscous Fluxes:** While the GPU kernels do the heavy lifting, it is good practice to define the Python reference implementations of the viscous stress tensor and heat flux here for validation or initial condition setup.
*   **Transport Coefficients:** Add definitions for dynamic viscosity ($\mu$) and thermal conductivity ($k$), potentially temperature-dependent (Sutherland's law).

### 4. `run_simulation.py` & Configs
*   **Parameters:** Add Reynolds number ($Re$) or viscosity to the configuration loading.
*   **BC Configuration:** Support new boundary types like `"no_slip_wall"` in the input parsing.

### Summary
You are essentially adding a second "pass" over the mesh to calculating gradients before the main flux pass, and updating the flux formulas to include viscosity. Most work lies in **`warp_kernels.py`** (math) and **`solver.py`** (orchestration).

✨ ## MODEL

To split the code effectively for supporting multiple equation systems (Euler, Navier-Stokes, Advection-Diffusion), you should adopt an **Strategy Pattern** where the physics logic is decoupled from the core Discontinuous Galerkin machinery.

Here is a proposed architecture:

### 1. New Directory Structure
Create a dedicated folder for the numerical methods (physics solvers):
```
src/
├── core/
│   ├── basis.py            # (Unchanged) Polynomial basis
│   ├── mesh.py             # (Unchanged) Mesh & Geometry
│   ├── driver.py           # (New) Abstract base class for explicit time-stepping
├── physics/
│   ├── base_solver.py      # (New) Abstract interface
│   ├── euler_2d.py         # (New) Euler-specific implementation
│   ├── navier_stokes_2d.py # (New) NS-specific implementation
├── kernels/
│   ├── common_kernels.py   # (New) Shared utils (Runge-Kutta, lifting, etc.)
│   ├── euler_kernels.py    # (New) Euler fluxes and equation kernels
│   └── ns_kernels.py       # (New) Viscous fluxes and penalty terms
```

### 2. Abstract Base Solver (`src/physics/base_solver.py`)
This class defines the "contract" that any physics model must fulfill. The core driver (time-loop) doesn't care if it's Euler or NS, it just needs to know how to compute `rhs`.

```python
class PhysicsSolver(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def compute_rhs(self, t, Q, rhs_buffer):
        """ Computes dQ/dt and stores it in rhs_buffer """
        pass

    @abstractmethod
    def calculate_dt(self, CFL):
        """ Returns the stable time step """
        pass
    
    @abstractmethod
    def apply_boundary_conditions(self):
        pass
```

### 3. Concrete Implementations

**`src/physics/euler_2d.py`:**
Contains the specific logic currently in `solver.py`.
- Initialization of Euler-specific variables.
- `compute_rhs` calls `euler_kernels.compute_volume` and `euler_kernels.compute_surface`.
- `calculate_dt` uses wave-speed estimation.

**`src/physics/navier_stokes_2d.py`:**
Contains the more complex multi-step logic.
- Initialization of Viscosity parameters.
- `compute_rhs` implements the two-step process:
    1. Call gradient kernel -> Store in `sigma`.
    2. Call diffusion flux kernel (using `Q` and `sigma`) -> Store in `rhs`.

### 4. Refactored `run_simulation.py` (The Factory)
The entry point essentially becomes a factory:

```python
# ... config loading ...

if config['physics'] == 'euler':
    solver = Euler2DSolver(mesh, basis, config)
elif config['physics'] == 'navier_stokes':
    solver = NavierStokes2DSolver(mesh, basis, config)

# Common Driver handles the time loop
driver = ExplicitTimeIntegrator(solver)
driver.solve(t_final, ...)
```

### Benefits
1.  **Isolation:** Changes to the Navier-Stokes kernels will never break the Euler solver.
2.  **Scalability:** Adding a "Maxwell Solver" or "Shallow Water Solver" just means adding a new file in `physics/` and `kernels/`.
3.  **Clarity:** `solver.py` currently mixes *orchestration* (RK loop) with *physics* (flux calls). Splitting them makes each file smaller and focused.

Get Neighbor Info\n        neighbor_e = connectivity[e, face_idx] \n        \n        # Loop over nodes on this face\n        for k in range(Nfp):\n            # Node Index on current element\n            node_idx_local = face_map[face_idx, k]\n            \n            q_inner = q[e, node_idx_local]\n            q_outer = q_inner # Default initialization\n            \n            if neighbor_e >= 0:\n                # --- Interior Face ---\n                # Find matching node on neighbor face.\n                # If I am face 1 (Right), neighbor sees me as face 3 (Left).\n                # Matching node ordering reverses (k -> Nfp-1-k).\n                neighbor_face = (face_idx + 2) % 4\n                \n                neighbor_node_idx = face_map[neighbor_face, k]\n                q_outer = q[neighbor_e, neighbor_node_idx]\n            else:\n                # --- Boundary Face ---\n                bc_type = bc_mask[e, face_idx]\n                \n                if bc_type == BC_WALL:\n                    # Slip Wall: Mirror velocity vector across the wall (remove normal component)\n                    # v_ghost = v - 2(v . n)n\n                    \n                    rho = q_inner[0]\n                    rhou = q_inner[1]\n                    rhov = q_inner[2]\n                    E = q_inner[3]\n                    \n                    # Momentum dot Normal\n                    mom_dot_n = rhou * nx + rhov * ny\n                    \n                    rhou_ghost = rhou - 2.0 * mom_dot_n * nx\n                    rhov_ghost = rhov - 2.0 * mom_dot_n * ny\n                    \n                    q_outer = wp.vec4(rho, rhou_ghost, rhov_ghost, E)\n                    \n                elif bc_type == BC_FARFIELD:\n                    # Extrapolation (Zero-Gradient / Transmissive)\n                    q_outer = q_inner\n                \n                else:\n                    # Default/Fallback\n                    q_outer = q_inner\n            \n            # 1. Numerical Flux (F*)\n            f_star = rusanev_flux(q_inner, q_outer, nx, ny)\n            \n            # 2. Normal Flux from interior (F_n)\n            f_n = flux_x(q_inner) * nx + flux_y(q_inner) * ny\n            \n            # 3. Flux Jump (F* - F_n) scaled by Surface Jacobian\n            flux_jump = (f_n - f_star) * surf_J\n            \n            # 4. LIFTing: Add contribution to ALL volume nodes\n            lift_col = face_idx * Nfp + k\n            \n            for i in range(q.shape[1]): # Iterate over all volume nodes (Np)\n                lift_val = LIFT[i, lift_col]\n                # Add to RHS: 1/J * LIFT * Jump\n                val = lift_val * flux_jump * inv_J\n                \n                wp.atomic_add(rhs, e, i, val)\n\n@wp.kernel\ndef rk_step(\n    q_old: wp.array(dtype=wp.vec4, ndim=2),\n    q_new: wp.array(dtype=wp.vec4, ndim=2),\n    rhs: wp.array(dtype=wp.vec4, ndim=2),\n    dt: wp.float32,\n    a: wp.float32, # RK parameter for q_old\n    b: wp.float32  # RK parameter for (q_new + dt*rhs)\n):\n    e, i = wp.tid()\n    q_new[e, i] = a * q_old[e, i] + b * (q_new[e, i] + dt * rhs[e, i])\n\n@wp.kernel\ndef compute_max_wave_speed(\n    q: wp.array(dtype=wp.vec4, ndim=2),      # Shape: (num_elements, Np)\n    max_speed: wp.array(dtype=wp.float32, ndim=1) # Shape: (1,)\n):\n    \"\"\"\n    Berechnet die maximale Wellengeschwindigkeit im gesamten Gebiet\n    und speichert das Maximum in max_speed[0].\n    \"\"\"\n    e, i = wp.tid()\n    \n    # Zustand laden\n    val = q[e, i]\n    rho = wp.max(val[0], rho_floor)\n    \n    # Primitive Variablen\n    u = val[1] / rho\n    v = val[2] / rho\n    p = pressure(val)\n    \n    # Schallgeschwindigkeit c\n    c = wp.sqrt(gamma * p / rho)\n    \n    # Betrag der Geschwindigkeit |u|\n    vel_mag = wp.sqrt(u*u + v*v)\n    \n    # Wellengeschwindigkeit lambda = |u| + c\n    wave_speed = vel_mag + c\n    \n    # Globales Maximum schreiben\n    # Hinweis: atomic_max funktioniert in neueren Warp-Versionen auch für floats.\n    wp.atomic_max(max_speed, 0, wave_speed)\n\n@wp.kernel\ndef rk_stage_1(\n    q: wp.array(dtype=wp.vec4, ndim=2),\n    rhs: wp.array(dtype=wp.vec4, ndim=2),\n    dt: wp.float32,\n    q_out: wp.array(dtype=wp.vec4, ndim=2)\n):\n    \"\"\"\n    Stage 1: Q(1) = Q_n + dt * RHS(Q_n)\n    \"\"\"\n    e, i = wp.tid()\n    q_out[e, i] = q[e, i] + dt * rhs[e, i]\n\n@wp.kernel\ndef rk_stage_2(\n    q: wp.array(dtype=wp.vec4, ndim=2),      # Q_n (Startzustand)\n    q_1: wp.array(dtype=wp.vec4, ndim=2),    # Q(1) aus Stage 1\n    rhs: wp.array(dtype=wp.vec4, ndim=2),    # RHS(Q(1))\n    dt: wp.float32,\n    q_out: wp.array(dtype=wp.vec4, ndim=2)   # Ziel für Q(2)\n):\n    \"\"\"\n    Stage 2: Q(2) = 3/4 * Q_n + 1/4 * (Q(1) + dt * RHS(Q(1)))\n    \"\"\"\n    e, i = wp.tid()\n    # 0.75 * Q_n + 0.25 * (Q_1 + dt * RHS)\n    q_out[e, i] = 0.75 * q[e, i] + 0.25 * (q_1[e, i] + dt * rhs[e, i])\n\n@wp.kernel\ndef rk_stage_3(\n    q: wp.array(dtype=wp.vec4, ndim=2),      # Q_n\n    q_2: wp.array(dtype=wp.vec4, ndim=2),    # Q(2) aus Stage 2\n    rhs: wp.array(dtype=wp.vec4, ndim=2),    # RHS(Q(2))\n    dt: wp.float32,\n    q_out: wp.array(dtype=wp.vec4, ndim=2)   # Ziel für Q(n+1) (überschreibt oft self.Q)\n    ):\n    \"\"\"\n    Stage 3: Q(n+1) = 1/3 * Q_n + 2/3 * (Q(2) + dt * RHS(Q(2)))\n    \"\"\"\n    e, i = wp.tid()\n    # 1/3 * Q_n + 2/3 * (Q_2 + dt * RHS)\n    q_out[e, i] = (1.0/3.0) * q[e, i] + (2.0/3.0) * (q_2[e, i] + dt* rhs[e, i])"
  }
}

```python
import warp as wp

@wp.kernel
def rk_stage_1(
    q: wp.array(dtype=wp.vec4, ndim=2),
    rhs: wp.array(dtype=wp.vec4, ndim=2),
    dt: wp.float32,
    q_out: wp.array(dtype=wp.vec4, ndim=2)
):
    """
    Stage 1: Q(1) = Q_n + dt * RHS(Q_n)
    """
    e, i = wp.tid()
    q_out[e, i] = q[e, i] + dt * rhs[e, i]

@wp.kernel
def rk_stage_2(
    q: wp.array(dtype=wp.vec4, ndim=2),      # Q_n (Startzustand)
    q_1: wp.array(dtype=wp.vec4, ndim=2),    # Q(1) aus Stage 1
    rhs: wp.array(dtype=wp.vec4, ndim=2),    # RHS(Q(1))
    dt: wp.float32,
    q_out: wp.array(dtype=wp.vec4, ndim=2)   # Ziel für Q(2)
):
    """
    Stage 2: Q(2) = 3/4 * Q_n + 1/4 * (Q(1) + dt * RHS(Q(1)))
    """
    e, i = wp.tid()
    # 0.75 * Q_n + 0.25 * (Q_1 + dt * RHS)
    q_out[e, i] = 0.75 * q[e, i] + 0.25 * (q_1[e, i] + dt * rhs[e, i])

@wp.kernel
def rk_stage_3(
    q: wp.array(dtype=wp.vec4, ndim=2),      # Q_n
    q_2: wp.array(dtype=wp.vec4, ndim=2),    # Q(2) aus Stage 2
    rhs: wp.array(dtype=wp.vec4, ndim=2),    # RHS(Q(2))
    dt: wp.float32,
    q_out: wp.array(dtype=wp.vec4, ndim=2)   # Ziel für Q(n+1) (überschreibt oft self.Q)
    ):
    """
    Stage 3: Q(n+1) = 1/3 * Q_n + 2/3 * (Q(2) + dt * RHS(Q(2)))
    """
    e, i = wp.tid()
    # 1/3 * Q_n + 2/3 * (Q_2 + dt * RHS)
    q_out[e, i] = (1.0/3.0) * q[e, i] + (2.0/3.0) * (q_2[e, i] + dt* rhs[e, i])

**Step 2: Create Solver Classes**

**2.1: `src/physics/base_solver.py`**
Abstract base class. It needs `mesh`, `basis`, `device`.
Methods:
- `initialize_q()`
- `compute_rhs(t, dt, q, rhs)`
- `calculate_dt(CFL)`

```python
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
import warp as wp

class BaseSolver(ABC):
    def __init__(self, mesh, basis, config=None):
        self.mesh = mesh
        self.basis = basis
        self.device = mesh.device
        self.config = config
        
        # State variables (to be initialized by concrete class)
        self.Q = None
        self.rhs = None
    
    @abstractmethod
    def initialize(self, initial_condition_func):
        """Initialize the state Q."""
        pass

    @abstractmethod
    def compute_rhs(self, t, dt, q, rhs):
        """Compute RHS = dQ/dt."""
        pass

    @abstractmethod
    def calculate_dt(self, CFL):
        """Calculate stable time step."""
        pass

from .base_solver import BaseSolver
from src.geometry.mesh import Mesh
from src.core.basis import Basis
from src.physics import equations as eq
from src.kernels import euler_kernels as wk # Renamed import
import numpy as np
import warp as wp

class Euler2DSolver(BaseSolver):
    def __init__(self, mesh, basis, config=None):
        super().__init__(mesh, basis, config)
        
        # --- Host-side data (for setup) ---
        self.geo_factors_host = np.zeros((mesh.num_elements, 5), dtype=np.float32)
        self.face_geo_factors_host = np.zeros((mesh.num_elements, 4, 3), dtype=np.float32)
        self.x_host = np.zeros((mesh.num_elements, basis.Np), dtype=np.float32)
        self.y_host = np.zeros((mesh.num_elements, basis.Np), dtype=np.float32)
        
        # Calculate geometric factors
        self._calculate_geometric_factors()
        self._map_nodes_to_physical_space()
        
        # BC Setup
        self._setup_boundary_conditions()

        # --- Device-side data ---
        self._update_device_metrics()
        
        self.x = wp.array(self.x_host, dtype=wp.float32, device=self.device)
        self.y = wp.array(self.y_host, dtype=wp.float32, device=self.device)

        # Mass Matrix
        weights_2d = np.kron(self.basis.weights_1d.numpy(), self.basis.weights_1d.numpy())
        M_inv_diag_host = 1.0 / weights_2d
        self.M_inv_diag = wp.array(M_inv_diag_host, dtype=wp.float32, device=self.device)
        
        # Wave speed buffer
        self.max_wave_speed = wp.zeros(1, dtype=wp.float32, device=self.device)

    def initialize(self, initial_condition_func):
        Q_host = np.zeros((self.mesh.num_elements, self.basis.Np, 4), dtype=np.float32)
        self._set_initial_conditions(Q_host, initial_condition_func)
        self.Q = wp.array(Q_host, dtype=wp.vec4, device=self.device)
        self.rhs = wp.zeros_like(self.Q)

    def compute_rhs(self, t, dt, q, rhs):
        rhs.zero_()
        
        # Volume
        wp.launch(
            kernel=wk.compute_volume_term,
            dim=(self.mesh.num_elements, self.basis.Np),
            inputs=[q, rhs, self.basis.Dr, self.basis.Ds, 
                    self.mesh.rx, self.mesh.ry, self.mesh.sx, self.mesh.sy, self.basis.Np],
            device=self.device
        )
        
        # Surface
        wp.launch(
            kernel=wk.compute_surface_term,
            dim=self.mesh.num_elements,
            inputs=[q, rhs, self.mesh.connectivity, self.basis.face_nodes, self.basis.LIFT,
                    self.face_geo_factors, self.mesh.J, self.bc_mask, self.basis.Nfp],
            device=self.device
        )

    def calculate_dt(self, CFL):
        self.max_wave_speed.zero_()
        wp.launch(
            kernel=wk.compute_max_wave_speed,
            dim=(self.mesh.num_elements, self.basis.Np),
            inputs=[self.Q, self.max_wave_speed],
            device=self.device
        )
        max_speed = self.max_wave_speed.numpy()[0]
        if max_speed < 1.0e-6: max_speed = 1.0 
        dt = CFL * self.mesh.dx / max_speed
        return dt

    # ... Helper methods (_calculate_geometric_factors, etc.) copied from DGSolver ...

**Step 3: Create `src/core/driver.py`**
This will contain the `TimeIntegrator` class (or similarly named) that replaces the `solve` method of `DGSolver`. It will use the `solver` (which is an instance of `BaseSolver`, e.g. `Euler2DSolver`) to compute RHS.

It needs to import `rk_stage_X` from `common_kernels`.

```python
import warp as wp
import os
import numpy as np
from src.kernels import common_kernels as ck

class TimeIntegrator:
    def __init__(self, solver):
        self.solver = solver
        self.device = solver.device
        
        # Allocate RK buffers
        # We assume solver has Q initialized
        self.Q_stage1 = wp.zeros_like(solver.Q)
        self.Q_stage2 = wp.zeros_like(solver.Q)
        
    def solve(self, t_final, CFL, log_frequency=10, writer=None):
        t = 0.0
        step = 0
        output_steps_dir = "data/steps"
        
        # Only create if writing to npz (no writer provided)
        if writer is None and not os.path.exists(output_steps_dir):
            os.makedirs(output_steps_dir)
            
        use_stream = self.device == "cuda"
        if use_stream:
            stream = wp.Stream(device=self.device)
            
        Q = self.solver.Q
        rhs = self.solver.rhs
        
        while t < t_final:
            dt = self.solver.calculate_dt(CFL)
            
            # --- RK3 Time Stepping ---
            # We call solver.compute_rhs(t, dt, q_in, rhs_out)
            # Then we call common RK kernels
            
            if use_stream:
                with stream:
                    # Stage 1
                    self.solver.compute_rhs(t, dt, Q, rhs)
                    wp.launch(kernel=ck.rk_stage_1, dim=Q.shape, inputs=[Q, rhs, dt], outputs=[self.Q_stage1], device=self.device)
                    
                    # Stage 2
                    self.solver.compute_rhs(t+dt, dt, self.Q_stage1, rhs)
                    wp.launch(kernel=ck.rk_stage_2, dim=Q.shape, inputs=[Q, self.Q_stage1, rhs, dt], outputs=[self.Q_stage2], device=self.device)
                    
                    # Stage 3
                    self.solver.compute_rhs(t+0.5*dt, dt, self.Q_stage2, rhs)
                    wp.launch(kernel=ck.rk_stage_3, dim=Q.shape, inputs=[Q, self.Q_stage2, rhs, dt], outputs=[Q], device=self.device)
                
                stream.synchronize()
            else:
                # Stage 1
                self.solver.compute_rhs(t, dt, Q, rhs)
                wp.launch(kernel=ck.rk_stage_1, dim=Q.shape, inputs=[Q, rhs, dt], outputs=[self.Q_stage1], device=self.device)
                
                # Stage 2
                self.solver.compute_rhs(t+dt, dt, self.Q_stage1, rhs)
                wp.launch(kernel=ck.rk_stage_2, dim=Q.shape, inputs=[Q, self.Q_stage1, rhs, dt], outputs=[self.Q_stage2], device=self.device)
                
                # Stage 3
                self.solver.compute_rhs(t+0.5*dt, dt, self.Q_stage2, rhs)
                wp.launch(kernel=ck.rk_stage_3, dim=Q.shape, inputs=[Q, self.Q_stage2, rhs, dt], outputs=[Q], device=self.device)
                
                wp.synchronize()
            
            t += dt
            step += 1
            
            if step % log_frequency == 0:
                q_np = Q.numpy()
                if np.isnan(q_np).any():
                    print(f"!!! Simulation unstable at step {step}")
                    break
                
                if writer:
                    writer.write_step(step, t, q_np)
                else:
                    # Legacy
                    np.savez(f"{output_steps_dir}/step_{step:04d}.npz", q=q_np) # Simplified
                
                print(f"Step: {step}, t = {t:.4f} / {t_final}, dt = {dt:.3e}")
```

🧑‍💻 ## USER

Can you explain me for every file why it is in the corresponding folder?

---

✨ ## MODEL

Here is an explanation of the file structure and why each file is located where it is:

### Root Directory
*   `run_simulation.py`: The **entry point** of the application. It resides in the root so users can easily run it (`python3 run_simulation.py`). It acts as the "Factory" that glues the components together based on the configuration.
*   `Agents.md`: Documentation for the AI (and developers) explaining the architecture and coding rules.
*   `.gitignore`: Defines what Git should ignore (like output data and temp files).

### `config/`
*   `default.yaml`: Stores default configuration settings. It's separated to allow users to have multiple configs without cluttering the root or source code.

### `meshes/`
*   (Empty by default): Intended place for storing user-generated mesh files (`.msh`).

### `scripts/`
*   `visualize.py`: Auxiliary scripts that are not part of the core simulation loop but help with pre- or post-processing.

### `src/` (Source Code)

#### `src/core/` (Core Infrastructure)
Contains the mathematical and structural backbone of the DG method, independent of specific physics (mostly).
*   `basis.py`: Defines the **Polynomial Basis** (Legendre polynomials, integration points, differentiation matrices). This is pure math required for any DG solver.
*   `driver.py`: Contains the `TimeIntegrator`. It handles the **Time Stepping Loop** (Runge-Kutta). It doesn't know about "Euler" or "Fluid", it just knows "compute RHS" and "update state". This allows the same driver to run any physics solver.

#### `src/geometry/` (Geometry Handling)
*   `mesh.py`: Handles **Mesh Loading and Topology**. It reads files (using `meshio`), manages vertices, connectivity, and maps Physical Groups (tags). It abstracts the grid away from the solver.

#### `src/physics/` (Physics Definitions)
Contains the high-level logic for specific physical equations.
*   `base_solver.py`: The **Interface (Abstract Base Class)**. It forces any new solver (like Navier-Stokes) to implement specific methods (`compute_rhs`, `calculate_dt`).
*   `euler_2d.py`: The **Concrete Implementation** for the Euler equations. It sets up the specific arrays needed for Euler (density, momentum, energy) and orchestrates the calls to the specific kernels.
*   `equations.py`: Pure Python reference implementations of the physics equations (fluxes, eigenvalues) used for initialization or debugging.
*   `initial_conditions.py`: Defines analytical initial states (like the Vortex) to set up the simulation.

#### `src/kernels/` (High-Performance Code)
Contains the **Nvidia Warp (CUDA/CPU)** kernels. These are the "heavy lifters" doing the actual math on the device.
*   `common_kernels.py`: Kernels that are **Equation-Independent**. The Runge-Kutta stages (`rk_stage_1`, etc.) just add vectors (`q_new = q_old + dt*rhs`) and don't care what the vectors represent.
*   `euler_kernels.py`: Kernels that are **Equation-Dependent**. `compute_volume_term` and `compute_surface_term` contain the specific flux formulas ($F(Q)$) for the Euler equations. If you added Navier-Stokes, you would add `ns_kernels.py` here.

#### `src/io/` (Input/Output)
*   `data_writer.py`: Handles writing data to disk (HDF5/XDMF). It isolates the I/O logic from the solver/driver, making it easier to change formats later (e.g., adding VTK support) without touching the physics code.

### `tests/`
*   `run_tests.py`: The global test runner.
*   `verification/`: Contains physics-based verification cases (like the Vortex test) that run the full simulation to ensure correctness.

    "output": "import numpy as np\nfrom scipy.special import legendre\nimport warp as wp\n\nclass Basis:\n    def __init__(self, polynomial_degree, device=\"cuda\", dtype=wp.float32):\n        self.N = polynomial_degree\n        self.N1 = self.N + 1\n        self.Np = self.N1 * self.N1\n        self.Nfp = self.N1\n        self.device = device\n        self.dtype = dtype\n\n        # Berechnung in float64 für Stabilität\n        nodes_1d, weights_1d = self._gauss_lobatto_quadrature(self.N)\n        \n        nodes_2d = self._create_2d_nodes(nodes_1d)\n        face_nodes = self._create_face_node_maps()\n        \n        # 1D Differentiationsmatrix\n        D1D = self._differentiation_matrix_1d(nodes_1d)\n        \n        # 2D Ableitungen\n        Dr, Ds = self._differentiation_matrices_2d(D1D)\n\n        # Massenmatrizen\n        # Die 2D Gewichte sind das Tensorprodukt der 1D Gewichte\n        # Da M diagonal ist, ist M_inv einfach 1/weights\n        weights_2d = np.kron(weights_1d, weights_1d)\n        inv_mass_matrix_diag = 1.0 / weights_2d\n\n        # Surface Mass Matrix (für die Integration auf den Kanten)\n        M_face = np.diag(weights_1d)\n\n        # LIFT Matrix erstellen (inklusive Inverser Massenmatrix!)\n        LIFT = self._create_lift_matrix(face_nodes, M_face, inv_mass_matrix_diag)\n        \n        # Transfer zu Warp (ggf. casten zu float32 hier)\n        self.nodes_1d = wp.array(nodes_1d, dtype=dtype, device=device)\n        self.weights_1d = wp.array(weights_1d, dtype=dtype, device=device)\n        self.nodes_2d = wp.array(nodes_2d, dtype=wp.vec2, device=device)\n        self.face_nodes = wp.array(face_nodes, dtype=wp.int32, device=device)\n        \n        # V1D brauchst du im Solver meist nicht, eher für Initialisierung/Filterung\n        # self.V1D = wp.array(V1D, dtype=dtype, device=device) \n        \n        self.D1D = wp.array(D1D, dtype=dtype, device=device)\n        self.Dr = wp.array(Dr, dtype=dtype, device=device)\n        self.Ds = wp.array(Ds, dtype=dtype, device=device)\n        self.LIFT = wp.array(LIFT, dtype=dtype, device=device)\n        \n        # Nützlich für CFL Bedingung\n        self.min_node_dist = np.min(np.diff(nodes_1d))\n\n    def _gauss_lobatto_quadrature(self, N):\n        if N == 0: return np.array([0.0]), np.array([2.0])\n        if N == 1: roots = np.array([])\n        else: roots = np.roots(legendre(N).deriv(1))\n        \n        nodes = np.concatenate(([-1.0], np.sort(roots), [1.0]))\n        weights = 2 / (N * self.N1 * legendre(N)(nodes)**2)\n        return nodes, weights\n\n    def _create_2d_nodes(self, nodes_1d):\n        # Meshgrid ist oft einfacher und weniger fehleranfällig\n        x, y = np.meshgrid(nodes_1d, nodes_1d)\n        # Warp erwartet oft Array of Structs (x, y), also (Np, 2)\n        return np.column_stack((x.flatten(), y.flatten()))\n\n    def _create_face_node_maps(self):\n        # Deine Map-Logik war korrekt für das Flattening row-major (Standard Numpy)\n        # Face 0 (bottom, y=-1), Face 1 (right, x=+1), etc.\n        # Aber Achtung: x changes fast, y changes slow in np.meshgrid('xy')? \n        # Prüfe Konsistenz mit _create_2d_nodes.\n        # Bei meshgrid default ist x row, y col.\n        # Hier behalten wir deine Logik bei, da sie konsistent wirkte.\n        face_nodes = np.zeros((4, self.Nfp), dtype=np.int32)\n        face_nodes[0, :] = np.arange(self.N1) # Bottom\n        face_nodes[1, :] = np.arange(self.N1-1, self.Np, self.N1) # Right\n        face_nodes[2, :] = np.arange(self.Np - self.N1, self.Np) # Top\n        face_nodes[3, :] = np.arange(0, self.Np - self.N1 + 1, self.N1) # Left\n        return face_nodes\n\n    def _differentiation_matrix_1d(self, nodes):\n        # KORRIGIERT\n        D = np.zeros((self.N1, self.N1))\n        for i in range(self.N1):\n            for j in range(self.N1):\n                if i != j:\n                    Ln_i = legendre(self.N)(nodes[i])\n                    Ln_j = legendre(self.N)(nodes[j])\n                    D[i, j] = Ln_i / (Ln_j * (nodes[i] - nodes[j]))\n                else:\n                    if i == 0:\n                        D[i, j] = -self.N * self.N1 / 4.0\n                    elif i == self.N:\n                        D[i, j] = self.N * self.N1 / 4.0\n                    else:\n                        D[i, j] = 0.0 # WICHTIG: 0 für Legendre!\n        return D\n\n    def _differentiation_matrices_2d(self, D1D):\n        I = np.eye(self.N1)\n        # Achtung: Reihenfolge hängt von deinem Flattening ab.\n        # Wenn nodes_2d via meshgrid/flatten erstellt wurde:\n        # Dr wirkt auf x (fast index) -> Kron(I, D)\n        # Ds wirkt auf y (slow index) -> Kron(D, I)\n        Dr = np.kron(I, D1D) \n        Ds = np.kron(D1D, I)\n        return Dr, Ds\n        \n    def _create_lift_matrix(self, face_nodes, M_face, inv_mass_matrix_diag):\n        \"\"\"\n        LIFT = M^(-1) * E\n        \"\"\"\n        # E Matrix: akkumuliert die Flux-Beiträge\n        E = np.zeros((self.Np, 4 * self.Nfp))\n        \n        for i in range(4):\n            # Indizes der Knoten auf Face i\n            f_idx = face_nodes[i, :]\n            \n            # Da wir Nodal-DG machen, ist die Projektion einfach:\n            # Wir schreiben die 1D Massenmatrix in die entsprechenden Zeilen von E\n            for k in range(self.Nfp):\n                row = f_idx[k]\n                col = i * self.Nfp + k\n                # Diagonaleintrag der Face-Massenmatrix\n                E[row, col] = M_face[k, k] # oder einfach weights_1d[k]\n\n        # Jetzt anwenden von M^(-1). Da M diagonal ist, skalieren wir einfach die Zeilen.\n        # Broadcasting: (Np, 1) * (Np, 4*Nfp)\n        LIFT = inv_mass_matrix_diag[:, None] * E\n        \n        return LIFT\n"
  }

Useful for CFL condition estimation\n        self.min_node_dist = np.min(np.diff(nodes_1d))\n\n    def _gauss_lobatto_quadrature(self, N):\n        \"\"\"\n        Computes Gauss-Lobatto-Legendre (GLL) nodes and weights.\n\n        Args:\n            N (int): Polynomial degree.\n\n        Returns:\n            tuple: A tuple (nodes, weights) containing numpy arrays of the quadrature points and weights.\n        \"\"\"\n        if N == 0: return np.array([0.0]), np.array([2.0])\n        if N == 1: roots = np.array([])\n        else: roots = np.roots(legendre(N).deriv(1))\n        \n        nodes = np.concatenate(([-1.0], np.sort(roots), [1.0]))\n        weights = 2 / (N * self.N1 * legendre(N)(nodes)**2)\n        return nodes, weights\n\n    def _create_2d_nodes(self, nodes_1d):\n        \"\"\"\n        Creates 2D nodal coordinates via tensor product.\n\n        Args:\n            nodes_1d (np.array): 1D GLL nodes.\n\n        Returns:\n            np.array: A (Np, 2) array containing (r, s) coordinates for all 2D nodes.\n        \"\"\"\n        # Meshgrid is simpler and less error-prone\n        x, y = np.meshgrid(nodes_1d, nodes_1d)\n        # Warp expects Array of Structs (x, y), so we stack them: (Np, 2)\n        return np.column_stack((x.flatten(), y.flatten()))\n\n    def _create_face_node_maps(self):\n        \"\"\"\n        Generates mappings from face indices to global 2D node indices.\n        \n        Assumes standard tensor-product ordering (row-major flattening).\n        Face 0: Bottom (y=-1)\n        Face 1: Right (x=+1)\n        Face 2: Top (y=+1)\n        Face 3: Left (x=-1)\n\n        Returns:\n            np.array: A (4, Nfp) integer array containing node indices for each face.\n        \"\"\"\n        face_nodes = np.zeros((4, self.Nfp), dtype=np.int32)\n        face_nodes[0, :] = np.arange(self.N1) # Important: 0 for Legendre GLL internal nodes\n        return D\n\n    def _differentiation_matrices_2d(self, D1D):\n        \"\"\"\n        Constructs 2D differentiation matrices using the Kronecker product.\n\n        Args:\n            D1D (np.array): The 1D differentiation matrix.\n\n        Returns:\n            tuple: (Dr, Ds), the differentiation matrices for r and s directions respectively.\n        \"\"\"\n        I = np.eye(self.N1)\n        # E Matrix: accumulates flux contributions from faces to volume nodes\n        E = np.zeros((self.Np, 4 * self.Nfp))\n        \n        for i in range(4):\n            # Indices of nodes on Face i\n            f_idx = face_nodes[i, :]\n            \n            # Right Tag\n\n                # Bottom (Face 0)\n                if j > 0:\n                    ni, nj = i, j - 1\n                    self.connectivity_host[element_id, 0] = [nj * self.nx + ni, 2]\n                else:\n                    self.boundary_tags_host[element_id, 0] = 1 # Bottom Tag\n\n                # Top (Face 2)\n                if j < self.ny - 1:\n                    ni, nj = i, j + 1\n                    self.connectivity_host[element_id, 2] = [nj * self.nx + ni, 0]\n                else:\n                    self.boundary_tags_host[element_id, 2] = 3 # Top Tag\n\n    def _load_from_file(self, filename):\n        \"\"\"\n        Loads an unstructured quadrilateral mesh from a file using meshio.\n\n        Args:\n            filename (str): Path to the mesh file (e.g., .msh).\n        \n        Raises:\n            ValueError: If no quadrilateral cells are found.\n        \"\"\"\n        mesh = meshio.read(filename)\n        \n        # Store Physical Groups Mapping: Name -> Tag\n        self.physical_groups = {}\n        if hasattr(mesh, 'field_data'):\n            for name, data in mesh.field_data.items():\n                # data is [tag, dim]\n                self.physical_groups[name] = data[0]\n        \n        print(f\"  Physical Groups: {self.physical_groups}\")\n        \n        # 1. Extract Quads\n        quads = None\n        for cell_block in mesh.cells:\n            if cell_block.type == \"quad\":\n                quads = cell_block.data\n                break\n        \n        if quads is None:\n            raise ValueError(\"No 'quad' cells found in the mesh file. This solver supports only Quadrilaterals.\")\n        \n        self.num_elements = len(quads)\n        print(f\"  Found {self.num_elements} quadrilateral elements.\")\n        \n        # 2. Vertices\n        # mesh.points usually 3D (x, y, z). We take x, y.\n        points_2d = mesh.points[:, :2]\n        \n        self.vertices_host = np.zeros((self.num_elements, 4, 2), dtype=np.float32)\n        # Copy vertex coordinates for each element\n        # quads is (NumElements, 4) indices\n        for i, cell in enumerate(quads):\n            self.vertices_host[i] = points_2d[cell]\n\n        # 3. Identify Boundary Edges from 'line' cells\n        # Map: tuple(sorted_nodes) -> physical_tag\n        boundary_edges = {}\n        \n        # Extract lines\n        lines = []\n        line_tags = []\n        \n        # Check where tags are stored (gmsh:physical is common)\n        # meshio structures varies: \n        # mesh.cell_data[\"gmsh:physical\"] is a list of arrays corresponding to mesh.cells blocks\n        \n        for i, cell_block in enumerate(mesh.cells):\n            if cell_block.type == \"line\":\n                data = cell_block.data\n                lines.append(data)\n                \n                # Try to get tags\n                if \"gmsh:physical\" in mesh.cell_data:\n                    line_tags.append(mesh.cell_data[\"gmsh:physical\"][i])\n                else:\n                    # Fallback or different format\n                    pass\n        \n        if lines:\n            lines_concat = np.concatenate(lines) if len(lines) > 1 else lines[0]\n            tags_concat = np.concatenate(line_tags) if len(line_tags) > 1 else line_tags[0]\n            \n            for edge, tag in zip(lines_concat, tags_concat):\n                key = tuple(sorted(edge))\n                boundary_edges[key] = tag\n                \n        print(f\"  Found {len(boundary_edges)} boundary edges with tags.\")\n\n        # 4. Connectivity (Dual Graph)\n        self.connectivity_host = -np.ones((self.num_elements, 4, 2), dtype=np.int32)\n        self.boundary_tags_host = np.zeros((self.num_elements, 4), dtype=np.int32)\n        \n        # Helper to identify faces: defined by sorted tuple of 2 node indices\n        # Face definitions for a quad (0,1,2,3):\n        # 0: 0-1 (Bottom)\n        # 1: 1-2 (Right)\n        # 2: 2-3 (Top)\n        # 3: 3-0 (Left)\n        face_defs = [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 0)]\n        \n        # Map: tuple(sorted_nodes) -> list of (element_id, face_idx)\n        face_map = defaultdict(list)\n        \n        for elem_idx, cell in enumerate(quads):\n            for local_face_idx, (n1_idx, n2_idx) in enumerate(face_defs):\n                # Global node indices\n                g1 = cell[n1_idx]\n                g2 = cell[n2_idx]\n                face_key = tuple(sorted((g1, g2)))\n                face_map[face_key].append((elem_idx, local_face_idx))\n        \n        # Build connectivity\n        for face_key, connections in face_map.items():\n            if len(connections) == 2:\n                # Internal face\n                (e1, f1), (e2, f2) = connections\n                self.connectivity_host[e1, f1] = [e2, f2]\n                self.connectivity_host[e2, f2] = [e1, f1]\n            elif len(connections) == 1:\n                # Boundary face\n                (e1, f1) = connections[0]\n                tag = boundary_edges.get(face_key, 0) # 0 if not found (should not happen if mesh is closed)\n                self.boundary_tags_host[e1, f1] = tag\n            else:\n                print(f\"Warning: Face {face_key} shared by {len(connections)} elements. Mesh might be non-manifold.\")\n        \n        # Calculate approximate grid size for dt estimation\n        # We take the sqrt of the average element area\n        # (This is a rough heuristic, max_wave_speed kernel handles local speed, but we need a length scale)\n        total_area = 0.0\n        for i in range(self.num_elements):\n            v = self.vertices_host[i]\n            # Area using Shoelace formula / cross product for convex quads\n            # d1 = v2 - v0, d2 = v3 - v1. Area = 0.5 * |d1 x d2|\n            d1 = v[2] - v[0]\n            d2 = v[3] - v[1]\n            area = 0.5 * np.abs(d1[0]*d2[1] - d1[1]*d2[0])\n            total_area += area\n            \n        avg_area = total_area / self.num_elements\n        self.dx = np.sqrt(avg_area) # Characteristic length\n        print(f\"  Approximate element size (dx): {self.dx:.4e}\")\n"
  }
}

Kinetische Energie: 0.5 * rho * (u^2 + v^2) = 0.5 * (rho_u^2 + rho_v^2) / rho\n    kin_energy = 0.5 * (rho_u*rho_u + rho_v*rho_v) / rho\n    p = (gamma - 1.0) * (E - kin_energy)\n    return wp.max(p, p_floor)\n\n@wp.func\ndef flux_x(q: wp.vec4) -> wp.vec4:\n    \"\"\"Flux function F(q) in x-direction.\"\"\"\n    rho = wp.max(q[0], rho_floor)\n    p = pressure(q)\n    u = q[1] / rho\n    \n    return wp.vec4(q[1], q[1]*u + p, q[2]*u, (q[3] + p)*u)\n\n@wp.func\ndef flux_y(q: wp.vec4) -> wp.vec4:\n    \"\"\"Flux function G(q) in y-direction.\"\"\"\n    rho = wp.max(q[0], rho_floor)\n    p = pressure(q)\n    v = q[2] / rho\n    \n    return wp.vec4(q[2], q[1]*v, q[2]*v + p, (q[3] + p)*v)\n\n@wp.func\ndef get_max_wave_speed(q: wp.vec4, nx: wp.float32, ny: wp.float32) -> wp.float32:\n    \"\"\"Calculates the acoustic wave speed |u_n| + c.\"\"\"\n    rho = wp.max(q[0], rho_floor)\n    p = pressure(q)\n    c = wp.sqrt(gamma * p / rho)\n    \n    # Velocity normal to the face\n    u_n = (q[1] * nx + q[2] * ny) / rho\n    return wp.abs(u_n) + c\n\n@wp.func\ndef rusanev_flux(q_l: wp.vec4, q_r: wp.vec4, nx: wp.float32, ny: wp.float32) -> wp.vec4:\n    \"\"\"Computes the Lax-Friedrichs / Rusanov numerical flux.\"\"\"\n    # Fluxes projected onto normal\n    F_l = flux_x(q_l) * nx + flux_y(q_l) * ny\n    F_r = flux_x(q_r) * nx + flux_y(q_r) * ny\n    \n    # Wave speeds\n    lambda_l = get_max_wave_speed(q_l, nx, ny)\n    lambda_r = get_max_wave_speed(q_r, nx, ny)\n    alpha = wp.max(lambda_l, lambda_r)\n    \n    # Numerical Flux: Avg(Flux) - Dissipation\n    return 0.5 * (F_l + F_r) - 0.5 * alpha * (q_r - q_l)\n\n# --- Solver Kernels ---\n\n@wp.kernel\ndef compute_volume_term(\n    q: wp.array(dtype=wp.vec4, ndim=2),      # (NumElems, Np)\n    rhs: wp.array(dtype=wp.vec4, ndim=2),    # Output RHS\n    Dr: wp.array(dtype=wp.float32, ndim=2),  # Differentiation Matrix r\n    Ds: wp.array(dtype=wp.float32, ndim=2),  # Differentiation Matrix s\n    rx: wp.array(dtype=wp.float32, ndim=1),  # Metric dr/dx\n    ry: wp.array(dtype=wp.float32, ndim=1),  # Metric dr/dy\n    sx: wp.array(dtype=wp.float32, ndim=1),  # Metric ds/dx\n    sy: wp.array(dtype=wp.float32, ndim=1),  # Metric ds/dy\n    Np: wp.int32                             # Number of points per element\n):\n    \"\"\"\n    Computes -div(F) using the strong form for general curvilinear coordinates:\n    div F = dF/dx + dG/dy\n    \n    Chain rule:\n    dF/dx = (dF/dr * dr/dx) + (dF/ds * ds/dx)\n    dG/dy = (dG/dr * dr/dy) + (dG/ds * ds/dy)\n    \n    rhs = - (dF_dx + dG_dy)\n    \"\"\"\n    e, i = wp.tid() # Element e, Node i\n\n    # Load Metrics for this element (constant for affine elements)\n    dr_dx = rx[e]\n    dr_dy = ry[e]\n    ds_dx = sx[e]\n    ds_dy = sy[e]\n\n    dF_dr = wp.vec4(0.0)\n    dF_ds = wp.vec4(0.0)\n    dG_dr = wp.vec4(0.0)\n    dG_ds = wp.vec4(0.0)\n\n    # Matrix-Vector Multiplication: Sum over j\n    for j in range(Np):\n        q_val = q[e, j]\n        \n        # Fluxes at node j\n        F_val = flux_x(q_val)\n        G_val = flux_y(q_val)\n        \n        # Accumulate derivatives\n        # We need derivatives of both fluxes with respect to both ref coords\n        dr = Dr[i, j]\n        ds = Ds[i, j]\n        \n        dF_dr += F_val * dr\n        dF_ds += F_val * ds\n        \n        dG_dr += G_val * dr\n        dG_ds += G_val * ds\n\n    # Apply Chain Rule\n    dF_dx = dF_dr * dr_dx + dF_ds * ds_dx\n    dG_dy = dG_dr * dr_dy + dG_ds * ds_dy\n    \n    # RHS update (Strong Form: rhs = -div F)\n    rhs[e, i] = -(dF_dx + dG_dy) \n\n\n@wp.kernel\ndef compute_surface_term(\n    q: wp.array(dtype=wp.vec4, ndim=2),        # State\n    rhs: wp.array(dtype=wp.vec4, ndim=2),      # RHS to accumulate into\n    connectivity: wp.array(dtype=wp.int32, ndim=2), # (NumElems, 4) -> NeighborID\n    face_map: wp.array(dtype=wp.int32, ndim=2),# (4, Nfp) -> Node Indices on faces\n    LIFT: wp.array(dtype=wp.float32, ndim=2),  # (Np, 4*Nfp) Lift Matrix\n    face_geo_factors: wp.array(dtype=wp.float32, ndim=3), # (NumElements, 4, 3) -> nx, ny, J_surf\n    J: wp.array(dtype=wp.float32, ndim=1),     # Volume Jacobian\n    bc_mask: wp.array(dtype=wp.int32, ndim=2), # (NumElements, 4) -> BC Type ID\n    Nfp: wp.int32                              # Number of face points\n):\n    \"\"\"\n    Computes the Flux Jump and Lifts it to the volume nodes.\n    Iterates over elements, calculates fluxes on all 4 faces, adds to RHS.\n    Supports unstructured meshes by reading normals and scaling from face_geo_factors.\n    Handles Boundary Conditions via bc_mask.\n    \"\"\"\n    e = wp.tid() # One thread per element\n\n    # Pre-load Volume Jacobian\n    vol_J = J[e]\n    inv_J = 1.0 / vol_J\n\n    # Loop over all 4 faces\n    for face_idx in range(4):\n        \n        # Load geometric factors for this face\n        nx = face_geo_factors[e, face_idx, 0]\n        ny = face_geo_factors[e, face_idx, 1]\n        surf_J = face_geo_factors[e, face_idx, 2]\n\n        # Get Neighbor Info\n        neighbor_e = connectivity[e, face_idx] \n        \n        # Loop over nodes on this face\n        for k in range(Nfp):\n            # Node Index on current element\n            node_idx_local = face_map[face_idx, k]\n            \n            q_inner = q[e, node_idx_local]\n            q_outer = q_inner # Default initialization\n            \n            if neighbor_e >= 0:\n                # --- Interior Face ---\n                # Find matching node on neighbor face.\n                # If I am face 1 (Right), neighbor sees me as face 3 (Left).\n                # Matching node ordering reverses (k -> Nfp-1-k).\n                neighbor_face = (face_idx + 2) % 4\n                \n                neighbor_node_idx = face_map[neighbor_face, k]\n                q_outer = q[neighbor_e, neighbor_node_idx]\n            else:\n                # --- Boundary Face ---\n                bc_type = bc_mask[e, face_idx]\n                \n                if bc_type == BC_WALL:\n                    # Slip Wall: Mirror velocity vector across the wall (remove normal component)\n                    # v_ghost = v - 2(v . n)n\n                    \n                    rho = q_inner[0]\n                    rhou = q_inner[1]\n                    rhov = q_inner[2]\n                    E = q_inner[3]\n                    \n                    # Momentum dot Normal\n                    mom_dot_n = rhou * nx + rhov * ny\n                    \n                    rhou_ghost = rhou - 2.0 * mom_dot_n * nx\n                    rhov_ghost = rhov - 2.0 * mom_dot_n * ny\n                    \n                    q_outer = wp.vec4(rho, rhou_ghost, rhov_ghost, E)\n                    \n                elif bc_type == BC_FARFIELD:\n                    # Extrapolation (Zero-Gradient / Transmissive)\n                    q_outer = q_inner\n                \n                else:\n                    # Default/Fallback\n                    q_outer = q_inner\n            \n            # 1. Numerical Flux (F*)\n            f_star = rusanev_flux(q_inner, q_outer, nx, ny)\n            \n            # 2. Normal Flux from interior (F_n)\n            f_n = flux_x(q_inner) * nx + flux_y(q_inner) * ny\n            \n            # 3. Flux Jump (F* - F_n) scaled by Surface Jacobian\n            flux_jump = (f_n - f_star) * surf_J\n            \n            # 4. LIFTing: Add contribution to ALL volume nodes\n            lift_col = face_idx * Nfp + k\n            \n            for i in range(q.shape[1]): # Iterate over all volume nodes (Np)\n                lift_val = LIFT[i, lift_col]\n                # Add to RHS: 1/J * LIFT * Jump\n                val = lift_val * flux_jump * inv_J\n                \n                wp.atomic_add(rhs, e, i, val)\n\n@wp.kernel\ndef compute_max_wave_speed(\n    q: wp.array(dtype=wp.vec4, ndim=2),      # Shape: (num_elements, Np)\n    max_speed: wp.array(dtype=wp.float32, ndim=1) # Shape: (1,)\n):\n    \"\"\"\n    Berechnet die maximale Wellengeschwindigkeit im gesamten Gebiet\n    und speichert das Maximum in max_speed[0].\n    \"\"\"\n    e, i = wp.tid()\n    \n    # Zustand laden\n    val = q[e, i]\n    rho = wp.max(val[0], rho_floor)\n    \n    # Primitive Variablen\n    u = val[1] / rho\n    v = val[2] / rho\n    p = pressure(val)\n    \n    # Schallgeschwindigkeit c\n    c = wp.sqrt(gamma * p / rho)\n    \n    # Betrag der Geschwindigkeit |u|\n    vel_mag = wp.sqrt(u*u + v*v)\n    \n    # Wellengeschwindigkeit lambda = |u| + c\n    wave_speed = vel_mag + c\n    \n    # Globales Maximum schreiben\n    # Hinweis: atomic_max funktioniert in neueren Warp-Versionen auch für floats.\n    wp.atomic_max(max_speed, 0, wave_speed)"

Optimierung: 0.5 * (rho_u^2 + rho_v^2) / rho ist numerisch stabiler \n    # als 0.5 * rho * (u^2 + v^2), da u=rho_u/rho -> u^2 = rho_u^2/rho^2\n    # Das spart eine Division und ist bei kleinem rho genauer.\n    kinetic_energy = 0.5 * (rho_u**2 + rho_v**2) / rho\n    p_val = (gamma - 1) * (E - kinetic_energy)\n    \n    return np.maximum(p_val, 1e-12)\n\ndef euler_fluxes(Q):\n    \"\"\"\n    Computes both F and G at once to save unpack operations/pressure calcs.\n    Returns F, G\n    \"\"\"\n    rho, rho_u, rho_v, E = Q\n    rho = np.maximum(rho, 1e-12)\n    p = pressure(Q)\n    \n    # Inverse density\n    inv_rho = 1.0 / rho\n    u = rho_u * inv_rho\n    v = rho_v * inv_rho\n    \n    # Flux F (x-dir)\n    f1 = rho_u\n    f2 = rho_u * u + p\n    f3 = rho_u * v     # rho_v * u ist das gleiche wie rho_u * v\n    f4 = (E + p) * u\n    \n    # Flux G (y-dir)\n    g1 = rho_v\n    g2 = rho_v * u     # rho_u * v\n    g3 = rho_v * v + p\n    g4 = (E + p) * v\n    \n    F = np.array([f1, f2, f3, f4])\n    G = np.array([g1, g2, g3, g4])\n    return F, G\n\ndef get_max_eigenvalue(Q, normal_vector):\n    rho = Q[0]\n    # Vermeide Division durch fast-Null\n    rho = np.maximum(rho, 1e-12)\n    p = pressure(Q)\n    \n    # Sound speed\n    c = np.sqrt(gamma * p / rho)\n    \n    nx, ny = normal_vector\n    # Velocity projected on normal\n    # u_n = (rho_u * nx + rho_v * ny) / rho\n    u_n = (Q[1] * nx + Q[2] * ny) / rho\n    \n    return np.abs(u_n) + c\n\ndef lax_friedrichs_flux(q_l, q_r, normal_vector):\n    \"\"\"\n    Computes the Lax-Friedrichs numerical flux projected on the normal.\n    \"\"\"\n    nx, ny = normal_vector\n    \n    # Compute fluxes\n    # Wir nutzen hier die kombinierte Funktion, um Rechenzeit zu sparen\n    F_l, G_l = euler_fluxes(q_l)\n    F_r, G_r = euler_fluxes(q_r)\n    \n    # Projected fluxes (Flux dot Normal)\n    flux_n_l = F_l * nx + G_l * ny\n    flux_n_r = F_r * nx + G_r * ny\n    \n    # Max eigenvalue (wave speed)\n    lambda_l = get_max_eigenvalue(q_l, normal_vector)\n    lambda_r = get_max_eigenvalue(q_r, normal_vector)\n    \n    # Global max wave speed at the interface\n    alpha = np.maximum(lambda_l, lambda_r)\n    \n    # Broadcasting Safety: alpha auf (1, N) bringen falls q (4, N) ist\n    # Das verhindert Fehler, falls die Dimensionen mal drehen\n    if alpha.ndim == 1:\n        alpha_b = alpha[None, :] \n    else:\n        alpha_b = alpha\n\n    # Numerical Flux Formula\n    # F_num = 0.5 * (F_L + F_R) - 0.5 * alpha * (Q_R - Q_L)\n    flux = 0.5 * (flux_n_l + flux_n_r) - 0.5 * alpha_b * (q_r - q_l)\n    \n    return flux\n\ndef primitive_to_conservative(prim):\n    \"\"\"\n    Converts primitive variables [rho, u, v, p] to conservative variables [rho, rho*u, rho*v, E].\n    \"\"\"\n    rho, u, v, p = prim\n    rho_u = rho * u\n    rho_v = rho * v\n    kinetic_energy = 0.5 * rho * (u**2 + v**2)\n    E = p / (gamma - 1) + kinetic_energy\n    return np.array([rho, rho_u, rho_v, E])\n\ndef conservative_to_primitive(Q):\n    \"\"\"\n    Converts conservative variables [rho, rho*u, rho*v, E] back to primitive [rho, u, v, p].\n    Used for visualization.\n    \"\"\"\n    rho, rho_u, rho_v, E = Q\n    \n    # Avoid division by zero\n    rho_safe = np.maximum(rho, 1e-12)\n    \n    u = rho_u / rho_safe\n    v = rho_v / rho_safe\n    p_val = pressure(Q) # Nutzt die bereits vorhandene pressure-Funktion\n    \n    return np.array([rho, u, v, p_val])"
  }
}

0.5 * alpha * (Q_R - Q_L)\n\n    Args:\n        q_l (np.array): State on the left side of the interface.\n        q_r (np.array): State on the right side of the interface.\n        normal_vector (tuple): Normal vector (nx, ny).\n\n    Returns:\n        np.array: The numerical flux vector.\n    \"\"\"\n    nx, ny = normal_vector\n    \n    # Compute fluxes\n    # We use the combined function to save computation time\n    F_l, G_l = euler_fluxes(q_l)\n    F_r, G_r = euler_fluxes(q_r)\n    \n    # Projected fluxes (Flux dot Normal)\n    flux_n_l = F_l * nx + G_l * ny\n    flux_n_r = F_r * nx + G_r * ny\n    \n    # Max eigenvalue (wave speed)\n    lambda_l = get_max_eigenvalue(q_l, normal_vector)\n    lambda_r = get_max_eigenvalue(q_r, normal_vector)\n    \n    # Global max wave speed at the interface\n    alpha = np.maximum(lambda_l, lambda_r)\n    \n    # Broadcasting Safety: ensure alpha has shape (1, N) if q is (4, N)\n    # This prevents errors if dimensions are flipped\n    if alpha.ndim == 1:\n        alpha_b = alpha[None, :] \n    else:\n        alpha_b = alpha\n\n    # Numerical Flux Formula\n    # F_num = 0.5 * (F_L + F_R) - 0.5 * alpha * (Q_R - Q_L)\n    flux = 0.5 * (flux_n_l + flux_n_r) - 0.5 * alpha_b * (q_r - q_l)\n    \n    return flux\n\ndef primitive_to_conservative(prim):\n    \"\"\"\n    Converts primitive variables [rho, u, v, p] to conservative variables [rho, rho*u, rho*v, E].\n\n    Args:\n        prim (np.array): Primitive variables.\n\n    Returns:\n        np.array: Conservative variables.\n    \"\"\"\n    rho, u, v, p = prim\n    rho_u = rho * u\n    rho_v = rho * v\n    kinetic_energy = 0.5 * rho * (u**2 + v**2)\n    E = p / (gamma - 1) + kinetic_energy\n    return np.array([rho, rho_u, rho_v, E])\n\ndef conservative_to_primitive(Q):\n    \"\"\"\n    Converts conservative variables [rho, rho*u, rho*v, E] back to primitive [rho, u, v, p].\n    Used for visualization and post-processing.\n\n    Args:\n        Q (np.array): Conservative variables.\n\n    Returns:\n        np.array: Primitive variables.\n    \"\"\"\n    rho, rho_u, rho_v, E = Q\n    \n    # Avoid division by zero\n    rho_safe = np.maximum(rho, 1e-12)\n    \n    u = rho_u / rho_safe\n    v = rho_v / rho_safe\n    p_val = pressure(Q) # Uses the existing pressure function\n    \n    return np.array([rho, u, v, p_val])\n"
  }

🧑‍💻 ## USER

Whats your opinion about putting inital and boundary conditions in its own folders?

---

✨ ## MODEL

Putting initial and boundary conditions into their own folders (e.g., `src/physics/initial_conditions/` and `src/physics/boundary_conditions/`) is generally a **good idea** as the project grows, but it depends on the complexity you anticipate.

**Pros:**
1.  **Scalability:** If you plan to add many different initial conditions (Kelvin-Helmholtz, Shock Tube, Sedov Blast, etc.) or complex BCs (Inlet profiles, Characteristic BCs), a single file becomes unmanageable.
2.  **Organization:** It keeps the file structure clean and makes it obvious where to look for specific physics setups.
3.  **Modularity:** You can have one file per case (e.g. `vortex.py`, `shock_tube.py`), which helps with version control and collaboration.

**Cons:**
1.  **Overhead:** For a small project with only 2-3 simple functions, it adds unnecessary directory depth and import complexity (`from src.physics.initial_conditions.vortex import vortex` vs `from src.physics.initial_conditions import vortex`).
2.  **Boilerplate:** You might need `__init__.py` files to expose the functions conveniently.

**My Opinion for *this* Project:**
Currently, you have:
*   `initial_conditions.py`: Contains 2 functions (`vortex`, `uniform`).
*   `boundary_conditions`: Logic is currently hardcoded in `solver.py` (mapping tags to IDs) and `warp_kernels.py` (implementing the math).

**Recommendation:**
1.  **Initial Conditions:** Keep them in `src/physics/initial_conditions.py` for now. Splitting into a folder is overkill unless you add >5-10 distinct cases.
2.  **Boundary Conditions:** This is where you *should* consider refactoring, but not necessarily into a folder of *Python* files yet. The complexity is in the **Kernels** (`warp_kernels.py`).
    *   If you add Navier-Stokes, you will need No-Slip, Adiabatic Wall, Isothermal Wall, Subsonic Inlet, etc.
    *   Moving the *math* of BCs out of the giant `compute_surface_term` kernel into separate `@wp.func` functions (e.g. in a `src/kernels/boundaries.py` or similar) would be a very strong architectural improvement.

**Verdict:**
*   **Initial Conditions:** Stay as is (single file).
*   **Boundary Conditions:** Refactor the *kernel implementation* into modular functions (Strategy pattern for kernels is hard, but `@wp.func` helps), but a folder structure for the *configuration* logic isn't needed yet.

If you foresee adding 10+ test cases, then yes, create `src/physics/initial_conditions/`. Otherwise, YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It).

✨ ## MODEL

I will refactor the boundary condition logic. Currently, the "logic" (mapping tags to IDs) is in `Euler2DSolver._setup_boundary_conditions` and the "math" (Slip Wall, Farfield implementation) is inside `src/kernels/euler_kernels.py` within the `compute_surface_term` kernel.

To "put boundary conditions in its own file," I essentially need to extract the **mathematical implementation** of the boundary conditions from the main surface kernel into a separate module, likely `src/kernels/boundary_conditions.py`. This will make `euler_kernels.py` cleaner and allow for easier addition of new BC types.

**Plan:**

1.  **Create `src/kernels/boundary_conditions.py`**:
    *   Define the BC Type constants (`BC_WALL`, `BC_FARFIELD`, etc.).
    *   Implement `@wp.func` functions for each BC type:
        *   `apply_slip_wall(q_inner, nx, ny)` -> `q_outer`
        *   `apply_farfield(q_inner)` -> `q_outer`
    *   Implement a dispatcher function `@wp.func` `apply_boundary_condition(bc_type, q_inner, nx, ny)` that calls the specific function.

2.  **Update `src/kernels/euler_kernels.py`**:
    *   Import the new BC functions (or the dispatcher).
    *   Replace the `if/else` block inside `compute_surface_term` with a call to the dispatcher or the specific functions.

3.  **Update `src/physics/euler_2d.py`**:
    *   Ensure it imports the BC constants from the new location (if I move them) or redefine them to match.

**Note on Warp Kernels:** Warp kernels generally need all code in one scope or imported. If I move functions to another file, I need to make sure `euler_kernels.py` can import them. Warp supports importing `@wp.func`.

    "content": "import warp as wp\n\n# --- Boundary Condition Type Constants ---\n# These must match the IDs used in the Solver configuration\nBC_INTERNAL = 0\nBC_WALL = 1      # Slip Wall (Euler)\nBC_FARFIELD = 2  # Non-reflecting / Outflow\n\n# --- Boundary Condition Functions ---\n\n@wp.func\ndef apply_slip_wall(q_inner: wp.vec4, nx: wp.float32, ny: wp.float32) -> wp.vec4:\n    \"\"\"\n    Applies Slip Wall boundary condition.\n    Mirrors the velocity vector across the wall surface (removes normal component).\n    \n    Args:\n        q_inner (wp.vec4): State inside the domain.\n        nx, ny (float): Normal vector pointing OUT of the domain.\n        \n    Returns:\n        wp.vec4: The ghost state q_outer.\n    \"\"\"\n    rho = q_inner[0]\n    rhou = q_inner[1]\n    rhov = q_inner[2]\n    E = q_inner[3]\n    \n    # Momentum dot Normal\n    mom_dot_n = rhou * nx + rhov * ny\n    \n    # Reflected momentum: v_ghost = v - 2 * (v . n) * n\n    rhou_ghost = rhou - 2.0 * mom_dot_n * nx\n    rhov_ghost = rhov - 2.0 * mom_dot_n * ny\n    \n    return wp.vec4(rho, rhou_ghost, rhov_ghost, E)\n\n@wp.func\ndef apply_farfield(q_inner: wp.vec4) -> wp.vec4:\n    \"\"\"\n    Applies Farfield / Outflow boundary condition.\n    Uses zeroth-order extrapolation (q_outer = q_inner).\n    \n    Args:\n        q_inner (wp.vec4): State inside the domain.\n        \n    Returns:\n        wp.vec4: The ghost state q_outer.\n    \"\"\"\n    return q_inner\n\n@wp.func\ndef apply_boundary_condition(bc_type: wp.int32, q_inner: wp.vec4, nx: wp.float32, ny: wp.float32) -> wp.vec4:\n    \"\"\"\n    Dispatcher for boundary conditions.\n    \n    Args:\n        bc_type (int): The boundary condition ID.\n        q_inner (wp.vec4): State inside.\n        nx, ny (float): Normal vector.\n        \n    Returns:\n        wp.vec4: The ghost state q_outer.\n    \"\"\"\n    # Default to inner state (transmissive)\n    q_outer = q_inner\n    \n    if bc_type == BC_WALL:\n        q_outer = apply_slip_wall(q_inner, nx, ny)\n    elif bc_type == BC_FARFIELD:\n        q_outer = apply_farfield(q_inner)\n        \n    return q_outer\n",
    "file_path": "src/kernels/boundary_conditions.py"
  }
}

Default initialization\n            \n            if neighbor_e >= 0:\n                # --- Interior Face ---\n                # Find matching node on neighbor face.\n                # Assuming conforming mesh where neighbors are matched:\n                # If I am face 1 (Right), neighbor sees me as face 3 (Left).\n                # Matching node ordering reverses (k -> Nfp-1-k) if orientations align standardly.\n                # Here we assume a standard mapping for simplicity.\n                neighbor_face = (face_idx + 2) % 4\n                \n                neighbor_node_idx = face_map[neighbor_face, k]\n                q_outer = q[neighbor_e, neighbor_node_idx]\n            else:\n                # Extrapolation (Zero-Gradient / Transmissive)\n                    q_outer = q_inner\n                \n                else:\n                    # Default/Fallback\n                    q_outer = q_inner\n            \n            # LIFTing: Add contribution to ALL volume nodes\n            lift_col = face_idx * Nfp + k\n            \n            for i in range(q.shape[1]): # Iterate over all volume nodes (Np)\n                lift_val = LIFT[i, lift_col]\n                # Add to RHS: 1/J * LIFT * Jump\n                val = lift_val * flux_jump * inv_J\n                \n                wp.atomic_add(rhs, e, i, val)\n\n@wp.kernel\ndef compute_max_wave_speed(\n    q: wp.array(dtype=wp.vec4, ndim=2),      # Shape: (num_elements, Np)\n    max_speed: wp.array(dtype=wp.float32, ndim=1) # Shape: (1,)\n):\n    \"\"\"\n    Computes the maximum wave speed in the entire domain for CFL calculation.\n    \n    This kernel iterates over all nodes, calculates |u| + c, and updates a global maximum using atomic operations.\n\n    Args:\n        q (wp.array): State vector array.\n        max_speed (wp.array): A scalar array (size 1) to store the result.\n    \"\"\"\n    e, i = wp.tid()\n    \n    # Load state\n    val = q[e, i]\n    rho = wp.max(val[0], rho_floor)\n    \n    # Primitive variables\n    u = val[1] / rho\n    v = val[2] / rho\n    p = pressure(val)\n    \n    # Sound speed c\n    c = wp.sqrt(gamma * p / rho)\n    \n    # Velocity magnitude |u|\n    vel_mag = wp.sqrt(u*u + v*v)\n    \n    # Wave speed lambda = |u| + c\n    wave_speed = vel_mag + c\n    \n    # Update global maximum atomically\n    wp.atomic_max(max_speed, 0, wave_speed)"

✨ ## MODEL

The new boundary condition logic works through a chain of 3 components: **Configuration**, **Mapping**, and **Kernel Execution**.

### 1. Configuration (`tests/verification/vortex_2D/vortex.yaml`)
You define the boundary conditions in the YAML file using the physical names (from Gmsh) and assigning a type.

```yaml
boundaries:
  "Left":
    type: "farfield"
  "Right":
    type: "farfield"  # ... etc
```

### 2. Mapping & Setup (`src/physics/euler_2d.py`)
In the `_setup_boundary_conditions` method of `Euler2DSolver`:
1.  The code reads the mesh file and `mesh.physical_groups` creates a map like `{"Left": 4, "Right": 2, ...}`.
2.  It reads your config and maps names to solver IDs:
    *   `"farfield"` -> `BC_FARFIELD` (Integer 2)
    *   `"slip_wall"` -> `BC_WALL` (Integer 1)
3.  It creates a `bc_mask` array (size `NumElements x 4`).
    *   For every element `e` and face `f`:
    *   If `mesh.boundary_tags[e, f]` corresponds to "Left" (Tag 4), it sets `bc_mask[e, f] = 2` (BC_FARFIELD).
    *   Internal faces remain `0`.

### 3. Kernel Execution (`src/kernels/euler_kernels.py` & `boundary_conditions.py`)
The `compute_surface_term` kernel runs on the GPU/CPU:

1.  It iterates over all faces.
2.  If a face has **no neighbor** (`neighbor_e < 0`), it checks `bc_mask[e, f]`.
3.  It gets the ID (e.g., `2` for Farfield).
4.  It calls `boundary_conditions.apply_boundary_condition(2, q_inner, ...)`:
    ```python
    # src/kernels/boundary_conditions.py
    if bc_type == BC_FARFIELD:
        q_outer = apply_farfield(q_inner) # Returns q_inner (transmissive)
    elif bc_type == BC_WALL:
        q_outer = apply_slip_wall(q_inner, nx, ny) # Returns mirrored velocity
    ```
5.  The returned `q_outer` (ghost state) is used to calculate the numerical flux `rusanev_flux(q_inner, q_outer, ...)`.

**In short:** The YAML string selects an Integer ID. That ID is stored in a mask array on the device. The Kernel reads the ID and calls the corresponding math function to generate the "ghost" state outside the domain.

**Step 2: Generate Mesh**
I'll create `tests/verification/channel_flow/generate_channel.py`.
Domain: [0, 10] x [0, 2].
Walls at y=0 and y=2.

```python
import gmsh
import sys
import os

def generate_mesh(filename):
    gmsh.initialize()
    gmsh.model.add("channel")

    L = 10.0
    H = 2.0
    lc = 0.5
    
    # Points
    p1 = gmsh.model.geo.addPoint(0, 0, 0, lc)
    p2 = gmsh.model.geo.addPoint(L, 0, 0, lc)
    p3 = gmsh.model.geo.addPoint(L, H, 0, lc)
    p4 = gmsh.model.geo.addPoint(0, H, 0, lc)

    # Lines
    l1 = gmsh.model.geo.addLine(p1, p2) # Bottom
    l2 = gmsh.model.geo.addLine(p2, p3) # Outlet
    l3 = gmsh.model.geo.addLine(p3, p4) # Top
    l4 = gmsh.model.geo.addLine(p4, p1) # Inlet

    cl = gmsh.model.geo.addCurveLoop([l1, l2, l3, l4])
    s = gmsh.model.geo.addPlaneSurface([cl])

    # Structured grid
    gmsh.model.geo.mesh.setTransfiniteCurve(l1, 21)
    gmsh.model.geo.mesh.setTransfiniteCurve(l3, 21)
    gmsh.model.geo.mesh.setTransfiniteCurve(l2, 6)
    gmsh.model.geo.mesh.setTransfiniteCurve(l4, 6)
    
    gmsh.model.geo.mesh.setTransfiniteSurface(s)
    gmsh.model.geo.mesh.setRecombine(2, s)

    gmsh.model.geo.synchronize()
    
    # Physical Groups
    gmsh.model.addPhysicalGroup(1, [l1], 1, "WallBottom")
    gmsh.model.addPhysicalGroup(1, [l2], 2, "Outlet")
    gmsh.model.addPhysicalGroup(1, [l3], 3, "WallTop")
    gmsh.model.addPhysicalGroup(1, [l4], 4, "Inlet")
    gmsh.model.addPhysicalGroup(2, [s], 10, "Domain")
    
    gmsh.model.mesh.generate(2)
    gmsh.write(filename)
    gmsh.finalize()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    generate_mesh("channel.msh")
